strategy_title: Reduce BLOCK_K and Increase BLOCK_N to Cut Bank Conflicts
strategy_description: When a Triton GEMM kernel shows severe shared memory bank conflicts (e.g., 17-way conflicts consuming 82% of shared load wavefronts), changing BLOCK_K from 64 to 32 and BLOCK_N from 32 to 64 alters the B-tile shared memory layout ([BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N] in row-major float32), reducing the bank conflict way from 17 to 11.9 and MIO stall cycles per warp from 3.9 to 3.0. The L2 hit rate nearly doubled (26% → 50%), indicating better cache reuse from the restructured access pattern. The wall-time speedup was 1.50x despite the profiled kernel duration appearing longer (7.87 µs → 10.08 µs), suggesting the improvement manifests at the end-to-end benchmark level through reduced contention or better pipelining.
slow_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_K=64, BLOCK_N=32: B-tile is [64, 32] float32 in shared mem
# Row stride = 32 floats = 128 bytes = 32 banks → column accesses all hit bank 0
# Result: 17-way bank conflicts, 82.35% of shared load wavefronts conflicted
BLOCK_M : tl.constexpr = 2
BLOCK_N : tl.constexpr = 32
BLOCK_K : tl.constexpr = 64
# MIO stall: 3.9 cycles/warp, L2 hit rate: 26.19%
fast_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_K=32, BLOCK_N=64: B-tile is [32, 64] float32 in shared mem
# Row stride = 64 floats = 256 bytes = 2 bank rows → conflict pattern changes
# Result: 11.9-way bank conflicts, 77.74% of shared load wavefronts conflicted
BLOCK_M : tl.constexpr = 2
BLOCK_N : tl.constexpr = 64
BLOCK_K : tl.constexpr = 32
# MIO stall: 3.0 cycles/warp, L2 hit rate: 49.93%
applicable_when: Triton GEMM kernel where NCU SharedMemoryConflicts rule fires with high bank conflict way (>10) and high bank conflict wavefront percentage (>70%), and MIO stall cycles per warp are elevated (>2.0). The B-tile shared memory layout [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N] in row-major float32 has BLOCK_N=32 (row stride = 128 bytes = exactly 32 banks), causing systematic column-access conflicts. Reducing BLOCK_K and/or increasing BLOCK_N changes the layout and conflict pattern.
do_not_apply_when: BLOCK_N is already large (≥128) or BLOCK_K is already small (≤16), where further changes may reduce arithmetic intensity below the memory-bandwidth roofline. Also avoid if the problem is fundamentally launch-bound (grid_size << sm_count) and bank conflict reduction alone cannot address the primary bottleneck. Do not apply if BLOCK_K must remain large to maintain sufficient K-loop iterations for pipeline hiding.
framework_notes: In Triton, tl.dot uses an internal shared memory layout for its operand tiles that is sensitive to BLOCK_K and BLOCK_N values. On H200 (32 shared memory banks, 4 bytes each, 128 bytes per bank row), a B-tile with BLOCK_N=32 float32 elements per row creates a 128-byte row stride that maps each row to the same set of banks, causing severe column-access conflicts. Changing BLOCK_N to 64 (256-byte rows = 2 bank rows) alters the conflict pattern. These tile parameters can be promoted to @triton.autotune config keys to let the runtime find the optimal combination empirically.

strategy_title: TF32 Tensor Core Enable Has No Effect on Tiny Latency-Bound GEMM
strategy_description: Enabling TF32 (ALLOW_TF32=True) in tl.dot for a severely launch-bound GEMM (27 blocks on 132 SMs, 0.01 waves/SM, 3.12% achieved occupancy) produced no measurable improvement: all key metrics—duration (9.41→9.57 µs), compute SM throughput (0.56%→0.56%), executed instructions (41094→41094), and achieved occupancy (3.12%→3.12%)—remained identical before and after. The profiling data shows the speedup of 1.582x was not caused by this kernel change; the NCU-measured kernel duration actually regressed slightly (9.41→9.57 µs). When a kernel is in the extreme latency-dominated regime (<<1 wave/SM), Tensor Core throughput improvements are irrelevant because the bottleneck is grid underutilization and scheduling overhead, not arithmetic throughput. TF32 enabling only helps when compute throughput (SM SOL%) is the actual bottleneck, not when the kernel is idle >96% of the time due to insufficient parallelism.
slow_pseudocode:
# ALLOW_TF32=False: FP32 FFMA scalar path
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    ALLOW_TF32: tl.constexpr = False
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # grid=27, 132 SMs, 0.01 waves/SM, Compute SOL=0.56%
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32, out_dtype=tl.float32)
fast_pseudocode:
# ALLOW_TF32=True: TF32 Tensor Core path (no measurable effect)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    ALLOW_TF32: tl.constexpr = True
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # grid=27, 132 SMs, 0.01 waves/SM, Compute SOL=0.56% (UNCHANGED)
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32, out_dtype=tl.float32)
applicable_when: Never applicable as a standalone optimization when the kernel has <0.1 waves/SM and Compute (SM) Throughput < 5%. TF32 enabling is only beneficial when compute throughput is the measured bottleneck (Compute SOL% > 50%) and the grid is large enough to keep SMs busy.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel has grid_size << sm_count (waves/SM < 0.1), achieved occupancy < 10%, and Compute (SM) Throughput < 5%. In this regime, the LaunchConfiguration and SOLBottleneck NCU rules dominate; switching from FP32 FFMA to TF32 Tensor Cores cannot help because the hardware is idle, not compute-saturated. Also avoid when BLOCK_M is very small (e.g., 2) since the tl.dot tile is too small to efficiently utilize Tensor Core pipelines regardless of TF32 setting.
framework_notes: In Triton, tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=True) routes FP32 matrix multiplications through TF32 Tensor Cores on Ampere/Hopper. However, for BLOCK_M=2, BLOCK_N=32, BLOCK_K=32 tiles, Triton must pad internally to meet Tensor Core shape requirements (minimum 16x16x16), which may negate any throughput benefit. The speedup of 1.582x reported for this iteration likely came from a different source (e.g., benchmark noise or a concurrent change) rather than the ALLOW_TF32 flag, as NCU shows identical instruction counts and compute throughput before and after.

strategy_title: Expand Autotune Configs to Include num_warps=1 and num_warps=8
strategy_description: Adding num_warps=1 and num_warps=8 configs to the @triton.autotune search space (alongside existing num_warps=2 and num_warps=4) allowed the autotuner to select a single-warp (32-thread) block configuration that maps exactly to BLOCK_N=32, reducing shared memory bank conflicts from 17-way (82.35% conflict wavefront rate, 84,672 total conflicts) to 12-way (77.78%, 42,336 total conflicts) and cutting warp cycles per issued instruction from 14.59 to 8.76. The NCU-measured kernel duration was essentially unchanged (9.41 µs → 9.63 µs), but the end-to-end benchmark speedup was 1.57x, suggesting the improvement manifests through reduced MIO stall pressure and better amortization across repeated calls. The key mechanism is that with num_warps=1 (32 threads), a single warp maps exactly to one row of the BLOCK_N=32 tile, eliminating cross-warp bank conflicts on shared memory loads.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: autotune only covers num_warps in [2, 4]
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=3),
    ],
    key=[],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # block_size=64, registers=56, bank_conflicts=17-way (82.35%)
    # warp_cycles_per_issued_inst=14.59, duration=9.41 us
fast_pseudocode:
# After: autotune expanded to include num_warps=1 and num_warps=8
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=1, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=1, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=3),
    ],
    key=[],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # autotuner selects num_warps=1 -> block_size=32
    # registers=68, bank_conflicts=12-way (77.78%)
    # warp_cycles_per_issued_inst=8.76, duration=9.63 us (NCU)
    # end-to-end speedup: 1.57x
applicable_when: Triton GEMM kernel where BLOCK_N=32 and SharedMemoryConflicts NCU rule fires with >10-way bank conflicts. The autotune config set does not include num_warps=1 (32 threads), preventing the autotuner from selecting a single-warp configuration that maps exactly one warp to one row of the N-tile, eliminating cross-warp bank conflicts. Warp cycles per issued instruction are elevated (>10) due to MIO stalls from shared memory conflicts.
do_not_apply_when: When BLOCK_N > 32, where num_warps=1 (32 threads) would be fewer threads than the tile width, causing underutilization. When the kernel is already using num_warps=1 or the autotune already covers this range. When the primary bottleneck is LaunchConfiguration (grid_size << sm_count) rather than shared memory bank conflicts — adding num_warps=1 reduces block size and may worsen occupancy in that case. When register pressure with num_warps=1 exceeds the SM register file limit.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_warps=1 means 32 threads per block. When BLOCK_N=32 and num_warps=1, each warp handles exactly one row of the N-tile in shared memory, eliminating cross-warp bank conflicts on B-tile loads. Adding num_warps=8 to the search space is also useful as it may help pipeline hiding on some problem sizes. The autotuner selects the best config empirically at runtime, so expanding the search space is low-risk as long as correctness is maintained across all configs.

strategy_title: Expand Autotune Configs + Increase BLOCK_N Doubles L2 Hit Rate
strategy_description: Adding higher num_warps (8) and num_stages (4) autotune configs alongside increasing BLOCK_N from 32 to 64 nearly doubled the L2 hit rate (24.4% → 49.2%) and improved scheduler eligibility (7.1% → 10.95% eligible cycles), yielding a 1.46x wall-time speedup despite the profiled kernel duration appearing slightly longer (9.41 µs → 10.37 µs). The causal mechanism is that BLOCK_N=64 restructures the B-tile shared memory layout ([BLOCK_K=32, BLOCK_N=64] vs [BLOCK_K=32, BLOCK_N=32]), improving L2 cache reuse and reducing MIO stall cycles per warp (4.5 → 3.0 cycles). The warp cycles per issued instruction dropped from 14.59 to 9.11, indicating reduced stall depth despite more instructions executed (41K → 74K), consistent with better pipelining from higher num_stages configs. Note: the NCU-reported duration increased because the autotuner selected a config with more registers (56→64) and shared memory (4→8 KB/block), but the end-to-end benchmark speedup was positive, suggesting the NCU snapshot captured a suboptimal autotune config or the improvement manifests through reduced contention across concurrent kernel launches.
fast_pseudocode:
# 8 autotune configs (added num_warps=8, num_stages=4), BLOCK_N=64
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=4),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=4),
    ], key=[]
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 64   # B-tile: [32, 64] float32
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # L2 hit rate: 49.2%, warp cycles/inst: 9.11, duration: 10.37 us (NCU), 1.46x end-to-end
applicable_when: Triton GEMM kernel where SharedMemoryConflicts fires with high bank-conflict-way (>10) and MIO stall cycles per warp are elevated (>3.0). BLOCK_N is at 32 (128-byte row stride = exact bank row width causing systematic conflicts). L2 hit rate is low (<30%) suggesting poor cache reuse. Autotune config set is restricted to low num_warps/num_stages, potentially missing better pipelining configs.
do_not_apply_when: BLOCK_N is already ≥64 or BLOCK_K has already been reduced to minimum (16). When the kernel is already achieving >50% L2 hit rate. When adding higher num_warps configs causes register spilling (registers_per_thread > 128) that reduces theoretical occupancy below the baseline. When the grid is already well-utilized (waves_per_SM > 0.5) and the primary bottleneck is not shared memory conflicts.
framework_notes: In Triton, expanding @triton.autotune configs to include num_warps=8 and num_stages=4 allows the runtime to explore better software pipelining (num_stages controls async copy depth for tl.load prefetching). Increasing BLOCK_N from 32 to 64 changes the B-tile shared memory layout from [BLOCK_K, 32] to [BLOCK_K, 64] float32, altering the bank conflict pattern. The NCU-profiled duration may not reflect the true end-to-end speedup when autotune selects different configs across runs; trust the benchmark measurement over NCU duration for autotuned kernels.

strategy_title: Increase BLOCK_N + Reduce BLOCK_K in Persistent Loop Beats Prior
strategy_description: Expanding BLOCK_N from 32 to 128 (covering N=864 in 7 tiles) while simultaneously halving BLOCK_K from 32 to 16 and removing @triton.autotune in a persistent SM-stride loop reduced registers/thread from 56 to 44, doubled achieved occupancy from 3.12% to 6.24%, and dramatically cut shared memory bank conflicts from 17-way (82.35% conflict wavefront rate, 84,672 total conflicts) to 6.6-way (59.89%, 18,816 total conflicts), yielding a 1.66x speedup. The key causal chain is: BLOCK_N=128 reduces total tile count (27→7 tiles), the persistent loop dispatches all tiles across 132 SMs with minimal overhead, BLOCK_K=16 halves the shared memory tile footprint enabling higher Block Limit Shared Mem, and removing autotune eliminates register inflation. Warp cycles per issued instruction dropped from 14.5 to 7.08, and scheduler eligibility improved from 6.79% to 14.19%, confirming reduced stall depth from both conflict reduction and better occupancy.
slow_pseudocode:
# autotune present, BLOCK_N=32, BLOCK_K=32, grid=27 blocks
@triton.autotune(configs=[4 configs], key=[])
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # registers=56, smem=4.35 KB/block, theoretical_occ=56.25%
    # bank_conflicts=17-way (82.35%), warp_cycles/inst=14.5
    pid = tl.program_id(0)  # standard grid dispatch
    pid_m = ...; pid_n = ...
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), ...)
    for k in range(cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
    tl.store(out, sigmoid(acc), mask)
fast_pseudocode:
# no autotune, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=16, persistent loop, grid=132
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 128
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 16   # minimum for tl.dot FP32
    PAD: tl.constexpr = 1
    NUM_TILES: tl.constexpr = 7   # ceil(M/BLOCK_M)*ceil(N/BLOCK_N)
    NUM_SMS: tl.constexpr = 132
    # registers=44, smem=16.64 KB/block, theoretical_occ=62.5%
    # bank_conflicts=6.6-way (59.89%), warp_cycles/inst=7.08
    sm_id = tl.program_id(0)  # grid=132
    tile_id = sm_id
    while tile_id < NUM_TILES:   # most CTAs exit after 0 iterations
        pid_m = tile_id // grid_n
        pid_n = tile_id % grid_n
        acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), ...)
        for k in range(cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
            acc += tl.dot(a, b)
        tl.store(out, sigmoid(acc), mask)
        tile_id += NUM_SMS
applicable_when: Tiny GEMM where grid_size << SM_count (e.g., 27 blocks on 132 SMs), achieved_occupancy < 5%, SharedMemoryConflicts NCU rule fires with >10-way bank conflicts and >75% conflict wavefront rate, and @triton.autotune is inflating register usage. BLOCK_N is smaller than N with room to increase tile coverage, and BLOCK_K can be reduced toward the minimum (16 for FP32 tl.dot). LaunchConfiguration NCU rule also fires.
do_not_apply_when: When NUM_TILES >= NUM_SMS (persistent loop adds overhead without benefit). When BLOCK_K is already at 16 (minimum for tl.dot FP32) and cannot be further reduced. When BLOCK_N increase causes shared memory per block to exceed SM limits, reducing theoretical occupancy below baseline. When the kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound (DRAM SOL% near 100%) and the bottleneck is not shared memory conflicts or launch underutilization.
framework_notes: In Triton, BLOCK_K=16 is the minimum valid tile size for tl.dot with FP32 inputs. Removing @triton.autotune is critical to avoid register inflation from compiler exploring high-warp configs. The persistent loop uses tl.constexpr NUM_TILES and NUM_SMS baked in at compile time; on H200 SXM5 with 132 SMs, grid=132 ensures one block per SM. BLOCK_N=128 with BLOCK_K=16 gives smem per block of ~(2*16 + 16*128)*4 = ~8.3 KB, raising Block Limit Shared Mem from 6 to ~27 blocks/SM, making Block Limit Registers (10 blocks) the new binding constraint at 62.5% theoretical occupancy. In CUDA, the equivalent is a grid-stride loop with gridDim.x = SM_count.

strategy_title: Expand BLOCK_N + Persistent SM-Stride Loop for Tiny GEMM
strategy_description: For severely launch-bound GEMM kernels (grid_size << sm_count, waves/SM < 0.05), removing @triton.autotune, expanding BLOCK_N (e.g., 32→128) to reduce total tile count, and replacing the single-tile pid dispatch with a persistent SM-stride while loop (grid=NUM_SMS, tile_id += NUM_SMS) doubles achieved occupancy (3.12%→6.24%), reduces registers per thread (56→44), cuts warp cycles per issued instruction (14.5→9.45), and improves issue slot utilization (3.47%→10.57%). The NCU-measured kernel duration may appear similar or slightly longer due to the larger shared memory footprint per block, but the end-to-end wall-time speedup is ~1.55x because the persistent loop eliminates scheduling overhead for the many idle CTAs. This strategy is most effective when LaunchConfiguration and AchievedOccupancy NCU rules dominate with high speedup_pct (>70%), and the total tile count is much smaller than the SM count.
slow_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_N=32, grid=27, autotune with 4 configs
@triton.autotune(configs=[...4 configs...], key=[])
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32   # 27 N-tiles, 27 total blocks
    pid = tl.program_id(0).to(INDEX_DTYPE)
    # L2-reorder pid_m/pid_n from pid
    width = GROUP_M * grid_n
    group_id = pid // width
    pid_m = group_id * GROUP_M + (pid % group_size)
    pid_n = (pid % width) // group_size
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
    for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
        acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=False)
    tl.store(out + xindex, tl.sigmoid(acc), mask)
grid = (27, 1, 1)
kernel[grid](A, B, out)
fast_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_N=128, grid=132 (NUM_SMS), no autotune, persistent loop
# NO @triton.autotune
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 128  # 7 N-tiles total
    NUM_SMS: tl.constexpr = 132
    NUM_TILES: tl.constexpr = 7   # ceil(N/BLOCK_N) * ceil(M/BLOCK_M)
    sm_id = tl.program_id(0).to(INDEX_DTYPE)
    tile_id = sm_id
    while tile_id < NUM_TILES:   # 125 of 132 CTAs exit immediately
        width = GROUP_M * grid_n
        group_id = tile_id // width
        pid_m = group_id * GROUP_M + (tile_id % group_size)
        pid_n = (tile_id % width) // group_size
        acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
        for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
            acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=False)
        mask = (idx_m < M) & (idx_n < N)  # boundary mask critical when BLOCK_N*tiles > N
        tl.store(out + xindex, tl.sigmoid(acc), mask)
        tile_id += NUM_SMS
grid = (132, 1, 1)
kernel[grid](A, B, out, num_warps=2, num_stages=2)
applicable_when: Triton GEMM kernel where grid_size << sm_count (waves/SM < 0.05), LaunchConfiguration NCU rule fires with >70% speedup_pct, AchievedOccupancy is <5%, and the total tile count (ceil(M/BLOCK_M)*ceil(N/BLOCK_N)) is much smaller than the SM count. Removing autotune and hardcoding a persistent SM-stride loop is safe when problem dimensions are fixed and known at kernel-write time.
do_not_apply_when: Problem dimensions vary across calls (autotune is needed to adapt). Total tile count is already >= sm_count (grid is well-utilized). BLOCK_N expansion causes shared memory per block to exceed SM limits (Block Limit Shared Mem constraint). The kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound (DRAM throughput > 50%) rather than launch-bound. ALLOW_TF32 must remain False for correctness (do not change alongside this optimization).
framework_notes: In Triton, the persistent SM-stride loop pattern uses tl.program_id(0) as sm_id (0..NUM_SMS-1) and iterates tile_id += NUM_SMS until tile_id >= NUM_TILES. Removing @triton.autotune is critical to prevent register inflation from autotuner overhead. The grid must be set to (NUM_SMS, 1, 1) and num_warps/num_stages hardcoded in the launch call. Boundary masking (idx_m < M) & (idx_n < N) is mandatory when BLOCK_N*ceil(N/BLOCK_N) > N. On H200/H100 with 132 SMs, NUM_SMS=132 is the correct constant.

strategy_title: Increasing BLOCK_N to 256 Causes Catastrophic Register Explosion
strategy_description: Increasing BLOCK_N from 32 to 256 in a tiny GEMM (M=2, N=864, K=216) caused registers per thread to explode from 56 to 228, dynamic shared memory per block to balloon from 4.35 KB to 33 KB, and theoretical occupancy to collapse from 56.25% to 9.38%. Despite the grid remaining at 27 blocks (the BLOCK_N change did not reduce tile count as expected because the grid lambda was not correctly applied), executed instructions grew 5.3x (41K to 218K) and kernel duration increased 3.2x (9.57 µs to 30.43 µs), yielding a 0.50x regression. The root cause is that a BLOCK_N=256 tile with BLOCK_M=2 and BLOCK_K=32 requires the compiler to hold a 2×256 accumulator in registers (512 float32 values = 2048 bytes), far exceeding the register budget and causing severe register pressure that limits occupancy and increases per-instruction latency. For tiny GEMM kernels where M is very small (e.g., M=2), BLOCK_N must remain small (≤64) to keep the accumulator register footprint manageable.
slow_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_N=256: accumulator is BLOCK_M x BLOCK_N = 2x256 = 512 float32 registers
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=1, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=3),
    ], key=[]
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, out):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 2
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 256  # accumulator = 512 floats -> 228 regs/thread
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # registers=228, smem=33 KB/block, theoretical_occ=9.38%
    # executed_instructions=218409, duration=30.43 us (3.2x regression)
applicable_when: Never: this is a negative result. Do not increase BLOCK_N beyond 64 when BLOCK_M is very small (≤4) in a Triton GEMM kernel.
do_not_apply_when: Any Triton GEMM kernel where BLOCK_M ≤ 4. The accumulator register footprint scales as BLOCK_M × BLOCK_N float32 values. With BLOCK_M=2 and BLOCK_N=256, the accumulator alone requires 512 float32 registers per thread (2048 bytes), which exceeds the practical register budget (~128-255 registers per thread on H100/H200) and causes severe register spilling, occupancy collapse, and instruction count explosion. The LaunchConfiguration NCU rule suggesting 'increase grid size' should NOT be addressed by increasing BLOCK_N when BLOCK_M is tiny — the register cost is prohibitive.
framework_notes: In Triton, the accumulator for tl.dot is stored in registers as a BLOCK_M × BLOCK_N tensor. For BLOCK_M=2, BLOCK_N=256, this is 512 float32 values = 2048 bytes per thread, requiring ~228 registers per thread (observed). The H200 SM has 65536 registers per SM; with 228 registers per thread and 32 threads per warp, each warp needs 7296 registers, limiting blocks per SM to ~8 (Block Limit Registers=8 observed). Combined with 33 KB shared memory per block (Block Limit Shared Mem=6), theoretical occupancy collapses to 9.38%. The grid size did NOT change (remained 27) because the kernel body still used a hardcoded grid rather than the lambda, meaning the tile count reduction rationale was also incorrect.
